name: Chainsoo
subtitle: garhwali black gram roasted and ground dry, then cooked to a smoky near-black mash

ingredients.note: the black skin is what gives chainsoo its colour
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Do not soak the dal. Chainsoo starts with dry roasting, and damp dal will steam in the pan instead of toasting.
Grind the roasted dal coarsely, to the texture of fine semolina rather than flour. Ground too fine it goes gluey.
Traditionally this is cooked in an iron kadhai, which is part of where the colour comes from. Use the heaviest pan you own.

steps.text: Dry roast the whole urad in a heavy kadhai over medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring constantly, until it smells nutty and a few grains crack.
steps.tip: Roast until dark and fragrant but never smoking. Scorched dal makes the whole pot bitter.

steps.text: Cool completely on a plate, then grind to a coarse meal.
steps.tip: Grinding hot dal releases oil and clumps the grinder. Give it 15 minutes.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, cut the heat for a minute, then crackle the cumin and red chillies.
Add the hing, garlic and ginger, and fry 90 seconds until the garlic turns pale gold.
Stir in the ground dal and roast it in the oil over low heat for 5 minutes, stirring the whole time. It will darken and smell toasty.
steps.tip: This second roast in oil is what separates chainsoo from ordinary dal. Keep the heat low and keep moving.

steps.text: Add the turmeric, coriander powder and chilli powder and fry 1 minute.
Pour in the hot water a ladle at a time, whisking after each addition so no lumps form.
steps.tip: Hot water, added gradually. Cold water straight in sets the ground dal into lumps you cannot break.

steps.text: Add salt and simmer uncovered on a low flame for 25 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until it is thick, glossy and almost black.
Stir in the garam masala, rest 5 minutes off the heat, scatter coriander and serve with plain rice.

storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It sets very firm — reheat with a good half cup of water, whisking until it loosens back to a pouring mash.
